subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 4. In this unit you will become fluent and confident with decimals – the numbers that carry a decimal point, such as 3.75, 0.6 and 12.045. You already meet decimals every day, often without noticing. When Amina counts out 147.50 shillings in change at the Hargeisa market, when Yusuf times his 100 metre sprint at 13.8 seconds, or when a trader in Mogadishu weighs 2.5 kilograms of bariis rice, they are all working with decimals. This year we go further than ever before: you will master all four operations with decimals, multiply and divide them with precision, convert smoothly between decimals and fractions, and solve multi-step real-world problems.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics 0862 — Stage 8 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Explain the place value of every digit in a decimal, including tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
Compare and order decimals accurately, even when they have different numbers of decimal places.
Add and subtract decimals by lining up the decimal points.
Multiply decimals, placing the decimal point correctly by counting decimal places.
Divide decimals, including dividing by a decimal, by converting to whole numbers.
Multiply and divide decimals by powers of 10 (10, 100, 1000) using the decimal-shift shortcut.
Convert fluently between fractions and decimals, and recognise terminating and recurring decimals.

concepts.title: Decimal Place Value
concepts.explanation:
Everything in this unit rests on one big idea: place value continues past the decimal point. To the left of the point you have the familiar places – ones, tens, hundreds. Each time you move one place to the left, the value is ten times bigger. Each time you move one place to the right, the value is ten times smaller. This pattern does not stop at the ones column. It simply keeps going, and the decimal point marks the boundary.

The first place after the point is tenths (each worth 1/10 = 0.1). The next is hundredths (1/100 = 0.01). The next is thousandths (1/1000 = 0.001). Consider the number 456.789. Reading from the left: the 4 is 4 hundreds, the 5 is 5 tens, the 6 is 6 ones. After the point, the 7 is 7 tenths, the 8 is 8 hundredths, the 9 is 9 thousandths. Written in full, 456.789 = 400 + 50 + 6 + 0.7 + 0.08 + 0.009.

Understanding place value lets you read any decimal correctly. In 0.0456, there is a 0 in the tenths place, a 4 in the hundredths place, a 5 in the thousandths place, and a 6 in the ten-thousandths place. The zero straight after the point is doing an important job: it is a place holder that keeps the 4 in the hundredths column. Without it, 0.0456 would collapse into 0.456, which is ten times bigger. Never drop a zero that sits between the decimal point and the other digits.

A very useful fact: a trailing zero at the very end of a decimal does not change its value. The numbers 0.5, 0.50 and 0.500 are all equal, because 5 tenths, 50 hundredths and 500 thousandths are the same amount. This is why, when Hassan writes a price as $4.50 rather than $4.5, the value is identical – he just chooses to show it to the hundredths (the cents) place. You will use trailing zeros constantly to keep your columns tidy when adding and subtracting.
concepts.example: Place value also carries the idea of precision. A length written as 12.3 cm is measured to the nearest tenth of a centimetre, while 12.30 cm claims precision to the nearest hundredth. In everyday maths the two are equal, but in science and engineering the extra zero says something about how carefully the measurement was taken. Keep this in mind whenever you meet measurements.

concepts.title: Comparing and Ordering Decimals
concepts.explanation:
To compare two decimals, examine their place values from left to right, starting with the largest place. Move rightwards only when the digits you are looking at are equal. The first place where the digits differ decides which number is greater.

Compare 3.456 and 3.465. The ones are equal (3 = 3). The tenths are equal (4 = 4). Move to the hundredths: 5 versus 6. Since 5 < 6, we conclude 3.456 < 3.465. We did not need to look at the thousandths at all, because the decision was already made.

The most common trap in the whole unit is thinking a decimal is bigger just because it has more digits. Compare 0.7 and 0.68. Some students say 0.68 is bigger because 68 is bigger than 7 – but that ignores place value. The safe method is to give both numbers the same number of decimal places by adding trailing zeros: write 0.7 as 0.70. Now compare 0.70 and 0.68. Both have 7 versus 6 in the tenths place – wait, 0.70 has 7 tenths and 0.68 has 6 tenths, so 0.70 > 0.68. Lining up the places makes the truth obvious.

To order a set of decimals, first write them all with the same number of decimal places, then compare column by column. Order 3.45, 3.4, 3.456 and 3.04 from least to greatest. Rewrite with three decimal places: 3.450, 3.400, 3.456, 3.040. Now the ordering is easy: 3.040, 3.400, 3.450, 3.456 – that is 3.04, 3.4, 3.45, 3.456. This tidy method never fails.
concepts.example: The same rules apply to negative decimals, but the order reverses, just as with negative whole numbers. Compare −2.3 and −2.7. The number closer to zero is the greater one, so −2.3 > −2.7. If the overnight temperature in the highlands near Hargeisa falls to −2.7°C one night and −2.3°C the next, the second night is the warmer one, even though 2.7 looks like the bigger figure.

concepts.title: Adding and Subtracting Decimals
concepts.explanation:
Adding and subtracting decimals uses one golden rule: line up the decimal points. Digits may only be combined with digits in the same place value column, so the points must sit directly under one another. Filling empty places with trailing zeros keeps the columns straight.

To add 23.456 + 7.89, stack the numbers so the points align and add a trailing zero to 7.89 so both have three decimal places:

Add column by column from the right, carrying whenever a column reaches ten, exactly as with whole numbers. The decimal point in the answer drops straight down from the points above it.

Subtraction works the same way, borrowing when needed. To calculate 45.7 − 18.93, write 45.7 as 45.70 so both numbers have two decimal places, then subtract: 45.70 − 18.93 = 26.77. When subtracting from a whole number, give it a decimal point and the zeros you need: 20 − 7.456 becomes 20.000 − 7.456 = 12.544.

Mental strategies can make simple sums faster. To work out 4.6 + 2.8, split each number into whole and decimal parts: (4 + 2) + (0.6 + 0.8) = 6 + 1.4 = 7.4. Breaking numbers apart like this often turns an awkward-looking sum into two easy ones.
concepts.example: Always estimate first to guard against silly slips. Before finding 23.456 + 7.89, round to 23 + 8 = 31, so the exact answer of 31.346 is clearly reasonable. If you had accidentally written 313.46, the estimate would immediately warn you that something went wrong. Estimation is your safety net throughout this unit.

concepts.title: Multiplying Decimals
concepts.explanation:
Multiplying decimals is easier than it looks, because you can ignore the decimal points at first. The method has three steps: multiply as whole numbers, count the decimal places, then place the point. The number of decimal places in the answer equals the total number of decimal places in the two numbers you multiplied.

Work out 2.3 × 1.4. Ignore the points and multiply 23 × 14 = 322. Now count decimal places: 2.3 has one, 1.4 has one, so the answer needs two decimal places. Place the point: 3.22. Check with an estimate: 2 × 1 = 2, and 3.22 is in the right region, so it is sensible.

Try a harder one: 3.45 × 2.6. Multiply 345 × 26 = 8970. Count decimal places: 3.45 has two, 2.6 has one, giving three decimal places, so the answer is 8.970, which we write as 8.97. Notice how the trailing zero was dropped once the point was placed. An estimate of 3 × 3 = 9 confirms the size is right.

Multiplying by powers of 10 has a beautiful shortcut. Multiplying by 10 moves the decimal point one place to the right: 4.56 × 10 = 45.6. Multiplying by 100 moves it two places: 4.56 × 100 = 456. Multiplying by 1000 moves it three places. Multiplying by 0.1, which is the same as dividing by 10, moves the point one place to the left: 4.56 × 0.1 = 0.456. Learn this pattern well – it saves enormous effort.

Fraction facts give handy mental shortcuts. Because 0.25 = 1/4, the calculation 0.25 × 8 is just 8 ÷ 4 = 2. Because 0.5 = 1/2, we get 0.5 × 6 = 6 ÷ 2 = 3. Spotting these connections makes you quick and confident.
concepts.example: Estimation is especially important in multiplication, because a misplaced decimal point changes the answer by a factor of ten or more. Before finding 4.7 × 3.2, estimate 5 × 3 = 15; the exact answer 15.04 sits right beside it, so you know the point is in the correct place. If your working had given 1.504 or 150.4, the estimate would flag the error at once.

concepts.title: Dividing Decimals
concepts.explanation:
Division of decimals splits into two cases. The first, and simpler, is dividing a decimal by a whole number. Divide as normal and keep the decimal point in the answer directly above the point in the number being divided. For example, 12.6 ÷ 3 = 4.2: the point in 4.2 sits above the point in 12.6.

The second case is dividing by a decimal, which needs one clever move. You cannot easily divide by 0.3, so first turn the divisor into a whole number. Multiply both numbers by the same power of 10, which keeps the answer unchanged. To calculate 8.4 ÷ 0.3, multiply both by 10: it becomes 84 ÷ 3 = 28. To calculate 15.75 ÷ 2.5, multiply both by 10 to get 157.5 ÷ 25 = 6.3. The rule is: shift the point in the divisor until it is whole, then shift the point in the dividend the same number of places.

Why does multiplying both numbers by 10 leave the answer the same? Because a division is really a fraction, and multiplying the top and bottom of a fraction by the same amount gives an equivalent fraction. 8.4 ÷ 0.3 is the fraction 8.4/0.3; multiply top and bottom by 10 and you get 84/3, the same value. Understanding this means you will never forget the method.

Dividing by powers of 10 mirrors multiplying. Dividing by 10 moves the decimal point one place to the left: 45.6 ÷ 10 = 4.56. Dividing by 100 moves it two places: 45.6 ÷ 100 = 0.456. This is the exact opposite of multiplying by 10, which moved the point to the right.
concepts.example: Sometimes a division does not stop neatly. When you calculate 22 ÷ 7 you get 3.142857…, which goes on forever. In such cases you round to a sensible number of decimal places for the situation: 3.14 for everyday work, or more places when great precision is needed. Always estimate first: 47.6 ÷ 3.8 is roughly 48 ÷ 4 = 12, confirming that the exact answer 12.5… is reasonable. Division is where estimation saves you most often.

concepts.title: Converting Between Fractions and Decimals
concepts.explanation:
Fractions and decimals are two ways of writing the same thing, and being able to swap between them freely is a powerful skill. To turn a fraction into a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator. The fraction 3/4 becomes 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75. The fraction 5/8 becomes 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625. The fraction 3/5 becomes 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6.

This division gives one of two results. A terminating decimal stops, like 0.75. A recurring (repeating) decimal goes on forever with a repeating pattern, like 1/3 = 0.333… or 1/7 = 0.142857142857…. There is a neat way to predict which you will get: if the denominator of the fraction, in its lowest terms, has only 2s and 5s as its prime factors, the decimal terminates; otherwise it recurs. This works because our number system is built on 10 = 2 × 5. So 1/2, 3/4, 7/8, 1/5 and 3/20 all terminate, while 1/3, 1/6 and 1/7 recur.

To turn a terminating decimal into a fraction, use place value to name it, then simplify. The decimal 0.375 is read as 375 thousandths, so it is 375/1000. Divide the top and bottom by their greatest common factor, 125, to get 3/8. Likewise 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20 after dividing by 5, and 0.6 = 6/10 = 3/5.

A mixed number combines a whole part and a fraction. The number 2 3/4 = 2 + 0.75 = 2.75. Going the other way, 3.25 = 3 + 0.25 = 3 + 1/4 = 3 1/4. Handling the whole part and the decimal part separately keeps this simple.
concepts.example: To compare a fraction and a decimal, put them in the same form. To compare 3/8 and 0.4, convert 3/8 to 0.375, then see that 0.375 < 0.4, so 3/8 < 0.4. Choosing whether to work in fractions or decimals is a real skill: measurements are usually easier as decimals (12.5 cm), while sharing and recipes often feel natural as fractions (half a cup). Fluency in both, and in converting between them, gives you the freedom to pick the easier path.

methods.title: How to multiply two decimals
steps: Ignore the decimal points and multiply as whole numbers.
Count the decimal places in each original number and add them.
Put that many decimal places into your answer.
Estimate to check the point is in the right place.

methods.title: How to divide by a decimal
steps: Multiply the divisor by 10, 100 or 1000 to make it a whole number.
Multiply the dividend by the same amount.
Divide as usual, keeping the decimal point lined up.
Estimate to check the answer is sensible.

methods.title: How to convert a fraction to a decimal
steps: Divide the numerator (top) by the denominator (bottom).
If it stops, it is a terminating decimal.
If a digit or block repeats forever, it is a recurring decimal.

methods.title: Multiplying decimals
steps: Solution: Ignore the points: 26 × 45 = 1170.
Count decimal places: 2.6 has one and 4.5 has one, giving two decimal places.
Estimate: 3 × 4 = 12, which confirms the answer.

methods.title: A clever multiplication
steps: Solution: Multiply as whole numbers: 125 × 16 = 2000.
Count decimal places: 0.125 has three, 16 has none, so three decimal places.
(You could also spot that 0.125 = 1/8, and 16 ÷ 8 = 2.)

methods.title: Dividing by a decimal
steps: Solution: Make the divisor whole.
Multiply both numbers by 10: 7.2 ÷ 0.9 becomes 72 ÷ 9 = 8.
Estimate to check: 7 ÷ 1 = 7, close to 8, so it is sensible.

workedExamples.title: Place value of a digit
workedExamples.prompt: In the number 67.459, what is the value of the digit 5?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: After the decimal point the places are tenths, then hundredths, then thousandths. The digits after the point are 4 (tenths), 5 (hundredths), 9 (thousandths). So the 5 is in the hundredths place and its value is 5 × 0.01 = 0.05.

workedExamples.title: Ordering decimals
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Give each three decimal places: 0.340, 0.304, 0.430, 0.034. Compare from the left. Smallest is 0.034, then 0.304, then 0.340, then 0.430. So the order is 0.034, 0.304, 0.34, 0.43.

workedExamples.title: Subtracting from a whole number
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Write 25 as 25.000 so both numbers have three decimal places. Line up the points and subtract: 25.000 − 12.345 = 12.655. Estimate to check: 25 − 12 = 13, close to 12.655, so it is reasonable.

workedExamples.title: Multiplying decimals
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Ignore the points: 26 × 45 = 1170. Count decimal places: 2.6 has one and 4.5 has one, giving two decimal places. So 1170 becomes 11.70 = 11.7. Estimate: 3 × 4 = 12, which confirms the answer.

workedExamples.title: A clever multiplication
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Multiply as whole numbers: 125 × 16 = 2000. Count decimal places: 0.125 has three, 16 has none, so three decimal places. 2000 becomes 2.000 = 2. (You could also spot that 0.125 = 1/8, and 16 ÷ 8 = 2.)

workedExamples.title: Dividing by a decimal
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Make the divisor whole. Multiply both numbers by 10: 7.2 ÷ 0.9 becomes 72 ÷ 9 = 8. Estimate to check: 7 ÷ 1 = 7, close to 8, so it is sensible.

workedExamples.title: Fraction to decimal
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Divide the numerator by the denominator: 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875. Because the denominator 8 = 2 × 2 × 2 has only 2s as factors, the decimal terminates – exactly as we predicted.

workedExamples.title: A money word problem
workedExamples.prompt: Sahra buys items costing $15.67, $9.89 and $12.45. She pays with a $50 note. How much change does she get?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: First add the costs: 15.67 + 9.89 + 12.45 = $38.01. Then subtract from 50: 50.00 − 38.01 = $11.99 change. Estimate: 16 + 10 + 12 = 38, and 50 − 38 = 12, close to $11.99, so it checks out.

workedExamples.title: Cost per kilogram
workedExamples.prompt: If 3.5 kg of apples costs 10.50 shillings, what is the cost per kilogram?
workedExamples.solution: Solution: Divide the total cost by the weight: 10.50 ÷ 3.5. Multiply both by 10: 105 ÷ 35 = 3. So the apples cost 3 shillings per kilogram.

activities.title: Receipt Detective
activities.materials: a real shopping receipt (or write out five prices yourself), paper and pencil.
steps: Copy down five prices from the receipt, each with two decimal places.
Estimate the total by rounding each price to the nearest whole unit and adding.
Now add the exact prices, lining up the decimal points carefully.
Compare your estimate with the exact total. How close were you?
Work out the change from a round amount (for example, 100 shillings or $50).

activities.title: Kitchen Measuring and Halving
activities.materials: a measuring cup or jug, water, and a simple recipe.
steps: Measure amounts such as 2.5 cups, 0.75 cups and 1.25 cups of water.
Write each amount as a fraction as well (2.5 = 2 1/2, 0.75 = 3/4, 1.25 = 1 1/4).
Halve the whole recipe by dividing each amount by 2.
Now make 1.5 times the recipe by multiplying each amount by 1.5.
Check: does doubling your 'half recipe' bring you back to the original amounts?

activities.title: The Decimal Place-Value Game
activities.materials: paper cards with the digits 0–9, and a home-made place value board (ones, point, tenths, hundredths, thousandths).
steps: Shuffle the digit cards and place them face down.
Each player draws four cards and arranges them on the board to make a decimal.
The player with the LARGER decimal wins the round – prove it by comparing place by place. (Playing alone or with your AI tutor? Deal two hands instead and compare 'Hand A' against 'Hand B'.)
Play again, but this time the SMALLER decimal wins.
Talk about the strategy: where should you place a large digit to make the biggest number?

activities.title: Best-Value Market Investigation
activities.materials: prices and weights of a few items (real or invented) from the market.
steps: Choose two packet sizes of the same food, for example 2.5 kg of rice and 1.5 kg of rice, each with a price.
For each packet, divide the price by the weight to find the cost per kilogram.
Compare the two cost-per-kilogram figures to decide which is better value.
Repeat with dates, sugar or camel milk sold in different sizes.
Write one sentence explaining how dividing decimals helps a family spend wisely.

activities.title: Stopwatch Sprint Times (Family or Group)
activities.materials: a phone stopwatch and a safe space to run or walk.
steps: Time each person over a short distance, recording seconds to two decimal places (for example 12.47 s). Practising alone? Time yourself over several attempts instead.
Order everyone's times from fastest to slowest by comparing decimals carefully.
Find the difference between the fastest and slowest time by subtracting decimals.
Add all the times together to find a 'team total' (or, if you are alone, add up your own attempts to find your 'personal total').
Try again after practice – did your times improve? By how many seconds?

activities.title: Fraction-Decimal Matching Pairs
activities.materials: paper to make a set of matching cards.
steps: Make cards for common fractions: 1/2, 1/4, 3/4, 1/5, 1/8, 3/8, 5/8.
Make matching cards for their decimals: 0.5, 0.25, 0.75, 0.2, 0.125, 0.375, 0.625.
Shuffle all cards face down and play a memory-matching game: turn over two and keep them if they are a pair.
For each pair you find, say aloud how you would convert one to the other by dividing.
Challenge: add a card for a recurring decimal such as 1/3 = 0.333… and discuss why it never ends.

rules.title: Place Value Rule
rules.text: After the decimal point the places are tenths, hundredths, thousandths. 0.4 = 4 tenths; 0.07 = 7 hundredths; 0.009 = 9 thousandths. Trailing zeros do not change the value: 0.5 = 0.50 = 0.500.

rules.title: Add and Subtract Rule
rules.text: Line up the decimal points, one under the other. Fill empty places with trailing zeros so both numbers have the same number of decimal places. Add or subtract as normal; the point in the answer drops straight down.

rules.title: Multiply Rule
rules.text: Multiply the digits as whole numbers, ignoring the points. Count the total decimal places in both numbers. The answer has that many decimal places.

rules.title: Divide Rule
rules.text: To divide by a decimal, multiply both numbers by 10, 100 or 1000 until the divisor is whole. Then divide as usual. Example: 8.4 divided by 0.3 becomes 84 divided by 3 = 28.

rules.title: Powers of 10 Rule
rules.text: Multiply by 10, 100, 1000: move the point 1, 2, 3 places RIGHT. Divide by 10, 100, 1000: move the point 1, 2, 3 places LEFT.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Converting Between Fractions and Decimals.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Fractions and decimals are two ways of writing the same thing, and being able to swap between them freely is a powerful skill. To turn a fraction into a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator. The fraction 3/4 becomes 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75. The fraction 5/8 becomes 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625. The fraction 3/5 becomes 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6.

This division gives one of two results. A terminating decimal stops, like 0.75. A recurring (repeating) decimal goes on forever with a repeating pattern, like 1/3 = 0.333… or 1/7 = 0.142857142857…. There is a neat way to predict which you will get: if the denominator of the fraction, in its lowest terms, has only 2s and 5s as its prime factors, the decimal terminates; otherwise it recurs. This works because our number system is built on 10 = 2 × 5. So 1/2, 3/4, 7/8, 1/5 and 3/20 all terminate, while 1/3, 1/6 and 1/7 recur.

selfAssessment: I can explain the place value of every digit in a decimal, including tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
I can compare and order decimals accurately, even when they have different numbers of decimal places.
I can add and subtract decimals by lining up the decimal points.
I can multiply decimals, placing the decimal point correctly by counting decimal places.
I can divide decimals, including dividing by a decimal, by converting to whole numbers.
I can multiply and divide decimals by powers of 10 (10, 100, 1000) using the decimal-shift shortcut.
I can convert fluently between fractions and decimals, and recognise terminating and recurring decimals.
